title: Identify your processes
goal: Find an owned process and explain its identity, parent and state.
challenge: Create a bounded owned process. Identify its PID, parent, owner and state; show a filtered and sorted process view. Explain why sleeping is not failure. Finish the practice process. Any equivalent Linux approach is acceptable.

steps.explanation: Start a ten-minute practice process. & returns the prompt.
steps.expected: Bash reports a job number and PID; record both. Do not assume either number.

steps.explanation: Immediately save the PID of the last background command.
steps.expected: No output. $p now identifies the sleep you just started.

steps.explanation: Inspect this specific process. PPID identifies its parent.
steps.expected: Your owned sleep appears, normally with S (sleeping). PID values vary.

steps.explanation: Filter by effective user and sort descending by PID. This is a snapshot.
steps.expected: Owned processes appear in descending PID order; ps can include itself.

steps.explanation: $$ is this Bash process. Compare it with sleep's PPID.
steps.expected: The parent relation explains how Bash launched sleep; processes and shell jobs are different views.

steps.explanation: Send TERM, then reap this shell's child.
steps.expected: For TERM-terminated sleep, Bash normally reports 143.

steps.explanation: Check that the practice process is gone.
steps.expected: Normally only the header remains; ps returns nonzero when no matching process exists.

hints: Save $! immediately after starting your own background process.
ps -p selects a PID; ps -u selects an effective user.
S means waiting/sleeping, while T means stopped. A changing snapshot is normal.
review: I matched a PID, owner and parent to my practice process.
I explained its state and a filtered, sorted view.
I terminated and reaped my practice process.
coverage: Real guest practice; completion is self-reviewed, with no guest assessment or verification score. Partial LPIC-1 103.5 coverage.
